title: Chapter 185 – Rebuilding
html:
[The Garden Hall, Council Room – Zhao]

Zhao learns, in the third week after the tide, that rebuilding is mostly arithmetic done by exhausted people before breakfast.

She sits at the head of the long council table in the pale light of a gray morning, with a bowl of Qinghe's broth going cold at her elbow and a tally-board propped against the inkwell. Her fingers are cracked. Her eyes burn. She has not slept more than four hours in any night since the Night of Counting, and her husband's chair, the plain oak one at her right hand, is still empty, because nobody has been able to bring themselves to take it away.

The board shows three columns. In the first, in her own hard upright hand: what we had. In the second: what we have. In the third, which is still blank, she has written one word, and underlined it twice. Need.

"Read it again," she says.

The new clerk clears her throat. Her name is Lian, and she is twenty, sharp-eyed, ink-fingered, plucked from the archive's lowest desk because Pei An once said she had a head for columns and no sense of occasion. She sits at the clerk's table with the great Roll open before her and a stylus tucked behind her ear, and she reads in the flat dry voice of someone who is afraid of dropping a plate.

"Grain. Eleven thousand measures at the start of the siege. Six thousand and four hundred now, after the kitchens and the tide. Oil, nothing. Lard, forty measures. Salt, eight hundred. Beans, two thousand. Dried fruit, nothing, the cellars flooded. Pickled radish, seven barrels." She turns a page. "Fuel. We have timber for perhaps five weeks. After that, the orchard stumps."

"And mouths?"

"Nine hundred and sixty-one on the Roll." Lian hesitates. "Plus the displaced."

"How many?"

"Nine hundred and forty-three. Counted at the Hall gate this morning."

A silence falls on the council table. Zhao looks around it. Six of them, in the gray light: Tian Mo, upright on a stool with his one hand on his knee; Ning Ruiyan, grimed to the wrists, with a roll of surveyors' plans; Sera, the new Captain, rigid as a post; Bell, hollow-eyed, sagging in her chair; Qinghe, at the end, with the black kettle in her lap; and Jian, in a corner by the fire, wrapped in a blanket with a cup of tea, looking like a man at a wake who has been told to keep quiet.

"Nine hundred and forty-three," repeats Zhao.

"The lower terraces," says Sera. "The river villages. Those who lost their houses and have no one left to take them in. They've been sleeping in the Hall corridors since the siege. I... they cannot be turned out, Clan Head. It is winter in six weeks."

"I know."

"And we cannot feed them."

"I know that, too."

She takes up the stylus. She stares at the third column, at the one word. She thinks of the shape of the numbers. A Garden that fed one thousand and some, and a winter of ninety days, and a store of grain that would, if shared out thin, last perhaps seven weeks for almost two thousand people.

"There is only one answer," she says slowly. "And I do not like it."

* * *

The argument lasts two hours, and it is the best two hours she has had in a month.

It is a real argument. That is the pleasure of it. For three weeks the council has done nothing but agree: yes, Clan Head, no, Clan Head, as you say, Clan Head, in the hushed dazed tones of people at a funeral. Now they are on their feet, all of them, shouting. It is wonderful.

"We cannot," says Ning Ruiyan, slapping her plans on the table. "We have no walls. I have measured them. The north curtain is a pile of rubble. The east gate is gone. If we take in nine hundred more and the beasts return, we will have nowhere to put them."

"The beasts will not return," says Tian Mo. "Not this season. The Alpha is dead."

"There are other Alphas."

"Seven," says Jian quietly, from the corner. "Seven leads remain. I will find them."

"With what time?" says Ning, wheeling on him. "Forgive me. With what time, Elder? If you are to find seven beasts, and unpick seven nails, I would like to know how many days of your life it costs, because I think the clan has a right to know what it is relying on."

Silence.

Jian sets down his cup. "Eleven weeks and some days," he says. "Less a day for each Scan."

"Then you cannot be our wall."

"No. I cannot." He meets her eyes. "I can only be the person who tells you where the wall should go."

Ning flushes. She sits down.

"There is a cost to the opposite choice," says Qinghe. Her voice is calm. She has not stood. She has not raised her voice since the meeting began, and the room goes quiet for her, as it always does. "If we turn them away, they will not go to the Sect. The Sect's gate is closed, and Head Han has a thousand of her own pupils to feed. They will go to the road. And the road in winter is a grave."

"That's not our responsibility," says Sera, harshly, and then flinches at her own words.

"No," says Qinghe. "It isn't. It is only our choice."

"Qinghe—"

"Hear me, Captain." The old cook rises. She stands at the end of the table with the kettle on her hip and her white hair bound in its cloth, small and bent and terrible. "I have been the clan's cook for a hundred years. I have never once turned a hungry person from my door. I have been tempted. In bad winters I have counted the grain and wished I could. But I have never done it, and I will not start now." She sets the kettle on the table with a flat clang. "I have a Core that feeds on appetite and returns it as healing. Do you understand what that means? Every bowl I serve makes the hungry stronger. The more mouths, the more broth, the more strength. I do not say it will stretch the grain. It will not. But it will stretch the people."

"By how much?"

"I do not know," says Qinghe. "I know only that I will not be the one to send them away."

* * *

At the end of the second hour, Zhao calls the question, and it goes against the arithmetic.

She had thought it might. She watches the hands go up, one by one, and feels the strange fierce pride she felt on the night of the drums. Tian Mo, first, with his one hand. Bell, slowly. Sera, after a long moment, with her jaw set and her eyes wet. Ning Ruiyan last, grudgingly, her face the color of a boiled beet.

"The Adoption Roll," says Zhao. "Under the old law. Any person who takes the name of the clan for a year and a day, and shares its labor and its bread, is a Lin. At the end of the year they may keep the name or return it. During the year, they eat what we eat."

"And when the grain runs out?" says Lian, in a very small voice.

"Then we will all eat less." Zhao lays down the stylus. "I propose a tithe. Every household, every family, down to the smallest, gives a fifth of what it holds. The Hall's stores give two-fifths. We will ration by the bowl, not by the head, and the cooks will serve from the same cauldron. No one eats separately. No one eats better. Is that understood?"

A murmur of assent.

"It will be a hungry winter," she says. "I will not pretend it will not. Some of us may die of it. I would rather die of hunger in the company of nine hundred who were fed, than live on a full belly knowing I had shut the door." She looks around the table. "If anyone disagrees, say so now. I will not hold it against you."

Nobody speaks.

"Then it is decided." She turns to the clerk. "Lian. Open the Roll to a clean page. Title it The Adoption of the Year of the Tide. We will begin at noon."

* * *

They line up in the great courtyard under a bleak white sky, and Zhao writes their names herself.

She does not have to. The clerk is there, with a stylus and a stool, and a second clerk sits beside her with a ruler. But Zhao has taken the Roll onto her knees, on the lowest step of the Hall, with the cold seeping through her robe, and she records every name in her own hard upright script. She wants to see their faces. She wants them to see hers.

They come in the dozens, and the hundreds. A woman with three children, all under six, and no husband. A boy of fourteen, with a bandaged hand, whose mother is in the black column. An old man with one leg and a crutch, who says his name is Ho and that he used to keep bees. A family of seven, grandparents to babies, who fled the river village with nothing but a bag of onions. A girl of twelve who says she has no parents and will not say more. A farrier, a weaver, a midwife, a man who cannot read, a woman who says she is an herbalist and produces, to prove it, a pouch of dried mullein.

Name?

Ho of the lower pasture.

Age?

Seventy-one.

Skill?

Bees, Clan Head. And I can mend a roof.

Welcome to the Lin clan.

She writes. The line moves. The pen scratches. The sky darkens, and the first flakes of snow begin to drift down across the courtyard, and still she writes. She has never felt so tired in her life. She has never felt so alive.

Around mid-afternoon, a small hand tugs at her sleeve.

It is a child, a girl of perhaps eight, in a ragged smock three sizes too large. She stands on the step beside Zhao with her chin tilted up and her eyes red and dry. She holds a tin cup in both hands.

"Mistress," she says. "Am I allowed to be a Lin?"

"Of course you are."

"I haven't got anyone."

"You have the clan now." Zhao dips the pen. "What is your name?"

The girl pauses. "Ping," she says.

Zhao's hand stops.

She looks down at the girl, at the dark eyes and the narrow chin and the stubborn set of the mouth. She thinks of a name in the black column, Ping, daughter of Hu, aged nine, in a clerk's careful hand, the last name Pei An ever wrote.

"Is that your own name?" she says softly.

"It was my sister's." The girl swallows. "She died in the cellar. I'd like to keep it. In case someone forgets."

Zhao puts down the pen.

She does not weep. She finds, in some bleak and wondering corner of herself, that she has none left. She only reaches out and takes the girl's face in both her cracked hands, and holds it for a moment, and then writes, below the last line on the page:

Ping. Of the lower pasture. Aged eight. Adopted into the Lin clan, in the name of her sister.

The girl looks at it a long time.

"Thank you," she says.

"Eat something," says Zhao, and her voice is unsteady. "Qinghe is in the kitchen."

* * *

The work begins at dawn, and she is on the north wall by the second hour.

It is a ruin. Ning was right. The curtain wall that Zhao's father raised in her girlhood has fallen in three places, great drifts of dressed stone strewn down the hill like toys. There is no mortar. There are no hoists. There is only the sky, and the cold, and eleven hundred people who have never laid a course of masonry in their lives, standing in lines at the foot of the slope with sacks on their shoulders and scarves wrapped round their faces.

She lifts a stone.

She is eighty-two. She has not lifted anything heavier than a ledger in twenty years. The block weighs perhaps forty pounds, and it grates against her palms, and she nearly drops it twice before she gets it up onto her shoulder. A young man nearby makes a startled sound.

"Clan Head, you shouldn't..."

"I know what I shouldn't." She hauls it three paces up the slope. "Move aside. I am in the way of my own wall."

He moves aside. She sets the block on the ruined course. It sits crookedly. She tries to adjust it, and fails, and a hand reaches past her and nudges it a half-inch into place. It is a big, scarred, patient hand, with the thick fingers of someone who has spent a lifetime with hives. Ho, of the lower pasture, grins at her through a gray beard.

"Beg your pardon, Mistress," he says. "But your lintel's off."

"It is a wall."

"It's all lintels if you're brave enough."

She laughs. She cannot help it. She steps back and watches the old beekeeper heave a second block into place with his one good leg planted firm. Beside him, a child hands up a trowel. Beside her, Sera has abandoned her Captain's dignity and is wrestling a rubble basket onto a boy's back. Farther along, Tian Mo works one-armed, steadying a beam with his shoulder while a pupil of the fifth landing drives a peg. The stone creature stands at the foot of the wall with its missing hand, patiently holding a ladder.

And at the far end, on the topmost course, a small green-eyed woman in a scorched blue gown is arguing with a surveyor's rope.

"No, no, no," Ning Ruiyan is shouting. "You have the angle wrong! It must lean back by one part in twelve! Do you want it to fall on someone?"

"It's not going to fall on anyone, ma'am."

"It will if you build it like that."

Zhao smiles. She wipes her forehead with her sleeve, leaving a streak of mud. The snow is falling in earnest now, soft and fine and white, settling on shoulders and hair and the raw gray stones of the wall. Nine hundred people and eleven hundred more work side by side, the old Lin and the new, and she cannot tell them apart.

It is a habit of getting up in the morning, she told Ning. We have done it before.

She had not believed it when she said it. She believes it now.

* * *

The Seven, to her surprise, turn out to be useful.

She had not expected it. She had expected to be a gracious host, to find them chairs and blankets and a corner of the infirmary, and to watch seven delicate prodigies from another world fade politely into the winter. Instead she finds that they work. They have been at Qinghe's table for ten days, eating twice a day, and the thread in them has stopped fraying, and now they are restless. They want to be employed. They go about the Garden in a loose cluster, barefoot in the snow because no one has yet found shoes small enough, and wherever they stop, something gets better.

Cheng Hui has taken over the archive. Zhao finds her there at noon, perched on a stack of ledgers in the dust with her spectacles on her nose, three clerks hovering at her elbow and a great fan of salvaged pages spread across the floor. She is reconstructing Pei An's index from memory. It is an extraordinary thing to watch. She reads a page once, and then lifts her eyes to the ceiling, and recites its contents in order, word for word, while the clerks scribble.

"The Court teaches you that," she says, noticing Zhao. "Or it did. I was nineteen when they took me. I could recite the whole of the Imperial Gazette from the Founding. It is a very dull book."

"And do you remember all of it?"

"Every word." She smiles, a thin wry smile. "It's both a gift and a disease."

Duan Ke has appointed himself to the walls. He stands on the north curtain from dawn to dusk with the pale blade across his back, glaring at the horizon, and says nothing to anyone. The guards fear him. Dai, who fears nothing, brings him tea. He drinks it without thanks. Zhao hears from Tian Mo that he has been drilling the fifth landing in the evenings, in the courtyard, with a wooden practice sword, without a word of instruction. They simply stand across from him, and he shows them what to do, and they do it.

"He fights like Jian," Tian Mo says. "The stance. The stillness. He's what Jian was at sixteen, if Jian had been angry."

"Was Jian never angry?"

"Not that I saw." Tian Mo hesitates. "That may have been his problem."

Zhen Li lights the lamps. It is the first thing he did, on the second day: he took his unlit lantern from the Dock and walked the Hall's corridors from cellar to roof, and wherever he stopped, a small steady flame appeared in the glass. It costs him something. She sees him pale a little every time. When she asks Bell what, the healer says only, a memory a night. Small ones. He chooses them himself. Zhao went to the boy that evening and tried to forbid it. He looked at her with grave, clear eyes and said, Clan Head, there are nine hundred new people in the Hall who are afraid of the dark. I am happy to be forgetting for them.

She did not forbid it. She still does not know whether that was mercy or cowardice.

And Tao, the five-year-old, runs through all of it like a loose spark, underfoot, tangled in aprons, followed everywhere by the three-year-old Ao and his rabbit. Wherever they go, children gather. By the third day, forty of the displaced young have attached themselves to the pair, a ragged, chattering procession. They play in the snow. They build a fort against the north wall. When Zhao passes, Tao waves a mitten and shouts Hello, Clan Head! and the forty shout it after him.

She waves back. She is surprised to find that she is smiling.

* * *

Jian finds her at dusk on the summit of the north curtain, where she is sitting alone on a block of fresh-laid stone with a cup of tea going cold.

He comes up the broken steps slowly, one hand on the staff, and sits beside her with a grunt that tells her what it costs. They look out over the valley. It is white. The ruined orchard, the burned terraces, the black scar where the tide went through, all of it softened by an inch of new snow into a calm and nameless country. Far to the north, a thread of smoke rises from the Valley Wall, where the Sect is mending its own.

"You're making a mistake," he says.

"Which one?"

"You are lifting stones."

"I am the Clan Head. I may lift what I please."

"You'll hurt your back."

"I have hurt my back every winter for forty years. It is a condition of the office." She sips the cold tea and grimaces. "Say what you came to say."

He is silent a while. The wind plays with the blanket on his shoulders.

"There is a thing I would like you to do," he says. "When I am gone."

"Jian."

"Hear me out. It is not sentimental." He turns his head, and she sees how thin the line of his jaw has become. "You are going to need an heir. Not for the Seat. For the Roll. Pei An is dead, Lan Wen is dead, your husband is dead. The clan has lost three of its oldest pillars in a week, and you are eighty-two. I think you should name someone now."

"Whom?"

"Kuang."

She stares at him.

"He's thirteen."

"He is thirteen and he asked me the truth, to my face, in front of the Dock. He held Yue's arm up when she couldn't stand. He carried water on the first night until his hands bled." Jian's voice is level. "He is not ready. But neither were you. Neither was I. He has the thing that matters, which is that he does not look away."

Zhao says nothing for a long moment. The snow drifts down between them.

"You think he would be good."

"I think he could be, with help. And I think he'd have it. Qinghe. Tian Mo. Bell. The Seven, if they stay." He lets out a long breath. "I will not be here to see it. That is the part I cannot bear. I would have liked to teach him the staff."

"You can teach him now."

"I'm not strong enough."

"Then teach him to sit beside you and watch you fail." Zhao's mouth twists. "It is a better lesson. I learned it from Dao."

Jian laughs. It turns into a cough. She waits until it passes, and puts her cracked hand over his bony one, and leaves it there.

"I will write it in the Roll tonight," she says. "As a note. Not a decree. The Clan Head names Lin Kuang as her successor, to be confirmed at the age of sixteen by the Council. Is that right?"

"That is exactly right."

"And you will sign it."

"If you'll let me."

"I will let you." She squeezes his hand. "You were the first of us to say we should keep the door open. I was wrong to argue."

"You were right to argue. It made me think."

"It did not make you change your mind."

"No," he says. "But it made me think."

They sit together until the light is gone.

* * *

The tally comes at midnight, and it is the one she has been dreading.

Lian brings it to her in the Roll Room, by lamplight, with the stylus behind her ear and her eyes wide. She lays the sheet on the desk. Zhao reads it standing, with her hands flat on the old wood where Pei An's spectacles still lie, and does the sum twice, in her head, and then a third time, on her fingers.

Mouths on the Roll: 1,904. Grain: 6,400 measures. Rate: one bowl per head, per day.

Days remaining: forty-one.

Winter: ninety.

She puts the sheet down.

She had known it. Of course she had known it. She did the arithmetic in her head in the council room, and the sum came out the same way, and she voted for it anyway. But there is a difference between knowing and seeing. The numbers lie on the desk in the lamplight, small and neat and indifferent, and she thinks, with a cold, steady, clear certainty: Forty-one days. And then we will have nothing.

"Clan Head?" says Lian, uncertainly.

"It is all right."

"Is there... will we..."

"We will manage." Zhao takes her stylus from the desk and holds it for a moment. "We will send to the Sect. Head Han will have grain. She has a granary the size of a hill. We will ask, and we will bargain." She sets down the pen. "And if she refuses, we will find a way."

"What if there isn't one?"

"There is always one." She lifts her eyes to the girl. "It is only a matter of what it costs."

She goes to the window. The snow has stopped. In the courtyard below, the Adoption Roll stands open on its desk beneath a lantern, nine hundred and forty-three names in her own hand, the ink still wet on the last page. Beyond it the wall rises dark against the stars, half-built, crooked, magnificent. And on its summit, small and gray and very far away, two figures sit side by side in the snow: a thin old man in a blanket, and a boy with a wooden sword.

She watches them for a long time.

Then she turns from the window and sits down at Pei An's desk, among his cracked spectacles and his dusty pens, and takes a slip of pale paper from the drawer.

"Lian," she says. "Fetch the pigeon-keeper."

"Now, Clan Head? It is the middle of the night."

"Now." Zhao dips the pen. She stares at the blank slip for a long moment, at the narrow white place where a begging letter ought to begin. She thinks of the way her mother's generation asked for favors, stating a need and leaving a neighbor to draw the conclusion. She finds she cannot bear it, and she finds she cannot think of another way.

"We will write to Head Han," she says. "We will tell her our numbers. We will ask for nothing."

"Nothing?"

"Nothing at all." Her mouth twists. "It is a very Lin way of asking."

The pen scratches. Outside, the snow begins again.
